title: Where dense retrieval fails: identifiers
summary: Embeddings are trained to put similar meanings close together, and that smoothing is exactly wrong for a string like SKU-4417, where 4418 is a different product rather than a similar one. Measured on a real tokeniser: two different SKUs share 60 percent of their tokens, the same as fox and dog.
html:
Yesterday BM25 answered a question about product codes with three lessons about product quantisation, because the word "product" was sitting in all of them. It matched a word instead of a meaning. Today is the mirror image, and it is the more dangerous of the two.

There is a family of queries that embeddings get wrong, reliably, and they all have the same shape: the query contains a string whose value is exact. A part number. An invoice number. An error code. A version string. A specific file path. An employee ID. For these, "close enough" is not a softer version of correct. It is simply wrong.

Smoothing is the feature, and here it is the bug

An embedding model is trained to put things that mean similar things near each other in space. That is the entire point, and it is why "the rate dropped" can match "interest rates fell" with no shared words. The model has learned to smooth over surface differences and keep the meaning.

Now ask it about SKU-4417. The model does what it was trained to do and places it near things that look and read like it, which includes SKU-4418. But 4418 is not a similar product. It is a different product. There is no sense in which it is a 99 percent correct answer.

The analogy I keep coming back to: an embedding is you describing a book to a librarian from memory. Brilliant for "the one about the whale, the captain is obsessed". Useless for "ISBN 978 0 14 243724 7", where only the exact digits matter and being one digit off is not being close.

Where it comes from, concretely

Models do not read characters. Text gets chopped into subword pieces first, and the model only ever sees the pieces. Here is what a real tokeniser, the one behind the OpenAI embedding models, does to two different part numbers:

SKU-4417     4 tokens    SKU | - | 441 | 7
SKU-4418     4 tokens    SKU | - | 441 | 8

Three of the four pieces are identical. The thing that distinguishes two unrelated products is one token out of four, and it is a lone digit, which in training data is close to meaningless. Compare:

SKU-4417    vs  SKU-4418         share 60% of their distinct tokens
INV-2024-00817 vs INV-2024-00818  share 71%
"the quick brown fox" vs "the quick brown dog"   share 60%

Two different SKUs look as similar to the model as fox and dog. The difference is that fox and dog really are similar, so the smoothing is right there and wrong here.

Note what that table is and is not. I measured the tokens, which are the model's input. I did not measure the embeddings themselves, because getting the model into this container is expensive. The published result, that dense retrievers lose badly to BM25 on exact-match queries, is well established and you should treat it as reported rather than as something I reproduced for you today.

Why this is worse than it sounds

A retrieval failure that returns nothing is annoying and obvious. This one returns the chunk about SKU-4418, which is a well formed, confident, plausible passage about a real product. The model then writes a fluent answer about the wrong item, and nothing anywhere in your pipeline raises a hand. You find out when a customer does.

If your corpus has identifiers in it, this failure is already happening and you have probably never seen it in an eval, because nobody writes eval questions containing part numbers.

What to actually do

Four options, roughly in order of how much they buy per unit of work.

Run a lexical index alongside the dense one and merge the results. BM25 handles exact strings and embeddings handle meaning, and almost nothing handles both. This is the standard answer and it is standard because it works. Tomorrow's lesson is Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which is how you merge two ranked lists without having to make their scores comparable.

Detect identifier shaped queries and route them. A regex for "contains a token with digits and punctuation mixed in" catches most of it. Send those to an exact lookup or a filtered query and skip the vector search entirely. Crude, cheap, and it removes the failure rather than softening it. Day 54 picks up routing properly.

Check your lexical tokeniser is not destroying the identifier too. Splitting on punctuation turns SKU-4417 into sku and 4417, and E_CONN_RESET into e, conn, reset. Now your supposedly exact index is matching on fragments as well. Keeping identifiers whole is a one line change to the tokeniser regex and it is the kind of thing people never check.

If the identifier is structured data, treat it as structured data. Put the SKU in a metadata field and filter on equality instead of searching for it. Days 29 and 30 were about what filters cost you, and this is the case where they earn it.

The option people reach for first, fine tuning the embedding model on their own identifiers, mostly does not work. You are asking a model built to generalise to memorise instead, and you have to redo it every time the catalogue changes. I will say plainly that this is my read rather than a settled result, but I have not seen a convincing version of it.

If you remember one thing
Embeddings smooth over surface detail, which is why they work. Identifiers are pure surface detail, so for those you need a lexical index, a filter, or a route, and not a better model.

Tomorrow: you have two ranked lists from two systems whose scores mean completely different things. Reciprocal Rank Fusion is the surprisingly simple way to combine them.
exercise:
One. Write your day 33 note. Days 31, 32 and 33 are all still open, so this is also me asking whether you are reading at all.

Two. Grep your own work codebase, or any repo you have handy, for strings that look like identifiers: grep -roE '[A-Z]{2,}[-_][A-Z0-9]{3,}' . | head -30. For three of them, ask whether a search engine that matched them 90 percent correctly would be useful or actively harmful. That is the whole lesson in one minute, on your own data.
